source.title: GRU: Mitigating the Trade-off between Unlearning and Retention for Large Language Models
source.authors: Yue Wang; Qi-Zhou Wang; Feng Liu; Wei Huang; Ya-Li Du; Xiaojiang Du; Bo Han

page_placements.theme: Forgetting-utility trade-off measured without any attack (method benchmarks and reruns)

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Evaluates unlearning and retention outcomes for established methods and the proposed GRU using benchmark measures, but does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports unlearning and retention outcomes on WMDP that bear on version A's unlearning-and-retention component. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, or prompting. Its gradient-alignment measurements describe the proposed method's training dynamics, not recovery of forgotten knowledge.
record.test_reason: GRU is a new unlearning method. The paper reports only removal and retention scores (WMDP QA, MMLU, TOFU FQ/MU, MUSE KnowMem) for its method against baselines. It runs no relearning, activation-ablation, quantization or prompting attack. Its results therefore cannot show whether unlearned knowledge is hidden or recoverable, which is what versions A–F turn on. Version A's defining element, that simple attacks fail to recover the knowledge, is never tested. GRU also makes no robustness claim, so it is not a version F counter-method. The WMDP numbers are the method's own performance compared with other methods, not a test of shallow unlearning.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that GRU mitigates the removal–retention trade-off across TOFU, WMDP and MUSE, and that it depends on retain-data quality. They also concede that on WMDP and MUSE retention gains sometimes cost slight removal strength, which they call negligible. The record's paraphrase omits this concession.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes Gradient Rectified Unlearning and task-vector rectification, and evaluates them with established unlearning baselines; it does not reproduce the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report benchmark- and method-dependent results, and select GRU hyperparameters by grid search on validation data. They report sensitivity to clipping threshold τ and EMA parameter γ on TOFU.

fits_no_version.finding: On WMDP with Zephyr-7B-beta, GA, WGA and GD bring Bio/Cyber to about 0.25 but also drop MMLU from 0.5814 to 0.245–0.26. Only NPO+GD (0.47–0.50) and RMU (0.41–0.44) keep more general ability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Near-chance WMDP accuracy from gradient-ascent-style unlearning often comes with collapse of general ability rather than targeted removal.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: No recovery attacks are tested. WMDP results use Zephyr-7B-beta; the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the tabulated outcomes. Some unlearning scores approach the stated floor while retention scores remain substantially below the original-model score.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the selected WMDP QA and MMLU results. TOFU and MUSE results are not included because their reported FQ, MU, and memorization measures do not directly report the targeted-knowledge accuracy and general-ability measures used for version A here.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the knowledge. Only post-unlearning accuracy is reported.
Activation ablation or access-vs-deletion analysis; not run. The gradient-cosine analysis concerns training dynamics.
Rephrasing, jailbreaks, languages or in-context recovery; not run.
GRU makes no robustness-to-attack claim and none is tested.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper whose WMDP comparisons include non-default RMU (alpha=100). No uncertainty estimates are reported. It belongs in T4: it uses unlearning methods and reports its own method's performance, not recovery.

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover the knowledge; the paper evaluates unlearning and retention, not post-unlearning recovery attacks.
Recovery through fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
Recovery by activation-direction ablation or evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Recovery through rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
The paper proposes GRU to mitigate the removal-retention trade-off, but does not test resistance to the attacks in versions B–E.

relation.reason: It evaluates its own method against established unlearning baselines and runs no recovery attack.

tranche.reason: The paper proposes a new unlearning method (GRU/TRU) and reports only removal and retention scores against baselines. It runs no relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting attack, so its results cannot show whether the knowledge is recoverable.

source_check.notes: All seven rows match Table 3 and Table 5. Table 5 (RMU) uses alpha=100, not the default 1200. It names no backbone and gives no original MMLU, but Section 5 sets Zephyr-7B-beta for WMDP and Table 3 gives 0.5814. The paper runs no recovery attack.

statements.correction: Table 3 (Zephyr-7B-beta, WMDP; original MMLU 0.5814): GA 0.2465, WGA 0.2454, GD 0.2589, NPO 0.3033 (0.3704 w/ GRU), NPO+GD 0.4724 (0.5033 w/ GRU). Table 5 (RMU, alpha=100 not default 1200): MMLU 0.41, 0.44 w/ GRU; RMU Bio 0.26, Cyber 0.31.
statements.problem: All numbers match Tables 3 and 5. But 'only NPO+GD and RMU keep more' leaves out NPO (MMLU 0.3033; 0.3704 w/ GRU). It also does not say that 0.50 and 0.44 are with-GRU values.

reader_labels.reason: Several methods bring Bio/Cyber scores close to the stated accuracy floor, but MMLU retention falls below the original 0.5814; GRU improves some retention scores without restoring them to the original level (r1–r30).
